items.title: My Husband Wants To Bring His Girlfriend To Thanksgiving. I’m Not Sure I’m Ready.
items.summary:
Welcome to Ask A MWLTF (Yes, that’s Mother Who Likes to F*ck.), a monthly anonymous advice column from Scary Mommy. Here we’ll dissect all your burning questions about motherhood, sex, romance, intimacy, and friendship with the help of our columnist, Penelope, a writer and mental health practitioner in training. She’ll dish out her most sound advice for parents on the delicate dance of raising kids without sacrificing other important relationships. Email her at askpenelope@scarymommy.com. 

Dear MWLF, 

My husband and I have been open for about two years. It was something we discussed carefully, and, for the most part, it has worked for us. We have rules, we communicate, and I’ve met a couple of the women he’s dated. I’m not interested in knowing every detail, but I also don’t feel threatened by the fact that he has relationships outside our marriage.

Now he’s been seeing someone for about six months, and he wants to bring her to Thanksgiving at my parents’ house.

We have two kids, and Thanksgiving is a big family holiday for us. My parents, siblings, nieces and nephews will all be there. My husband says he wants to stop treating this relationship like something that has to be kept separate from the rest of his life. He says he’s serious about her and thinks including her would make things feel more natural and less secretive.

I understand that. But I also feel strangely territorial. Thanksgiving is one of the few days of the year when I get to be with my whole family, and I don’t particularly want to spend it navigating my husband’s girlfriend. I’m worried about what…
items.t: My Husband Wants To Bring His Girlfriend To Thanksgiving. I’m Not Sure I’m Ready.

items.title: Nobody Warned Me About Bladder Leaks Before Becoming a Mom — Here's What I Wish I'd Known
items.summary:
After having my second baby, my body was a mess: hair falling out, boobs engorged — the works. So when I peed a little when I sneezed, it didn’t seem like a big deal. Until it happened again. And again. Eventually, I managed to sneeze, cough, and laugh without feeling some bladder leakage, but it took a few months for my body to get the memo.

These days, everyone talks about their pelvic floor: what it is, how to strengthen it, how having a baby can wreck it. But bladder leakage — which can be related to that all-important pelvic floor and the stress it undergoes during pregnancy and labor — tends to fly under the radar. No one wants to talk about it, maybe because there’s still a stigma attached to bathroom issues. Even though I’ve discussed every other postpartum thing under the sun (padsicles! Peri bottles! Nipple shields!) with my friends, urinary incontinence has never entered the chat. 

But fortunately, Poise is ready to. The brand’s variety of bladder-leakage pads makes it easy to find exactly what you want, be it feels-like-you’re-wearing-nothing protection or a pad that keeps you dry all day. With that, here’s everything I wish someone had warned me about ahead of time.

1. Bladder Leaks Are Super Common Bladder leakage might not come up a lot (or at all) in the group chat, but a lot of women experience it. In fact, a large scientific review found that one in three women experiences bladder leakage between six weeks and a year after giving birth — whether it’s their first child or their third. So you’re probably not the only mom at the baby music class who’s…

items.title: So You Think You Have Insomnia. What Now?
items.summary:
Ekaterina Goncharova/Moment/Getty Images When you’re a parent, it’s sometimes hard to tell what is a normal amount of tired and what’s an unhealthy level of exhaustion. Aren’t we all at least a little bit tired all the time? So when should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? But if you’ve been struggling night after night to fall asleep, you can’t seem to stay asleep, or you never feel well-rested in the mornings , it might be a sign that your sleep needs a little TLC. And yes, even if you’re hesitant to take medications to help you fall and stay asleep , there are actually other treatment options you can try.

Scary Mommy spoke with Dr. Jessica Meers , board-certified sleep psychologist and founder of Rhythm Wellness Sleep Solutions, to find out where you should turn for insomnia help first — and what treatment options even exist.

When should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? When does “I’m struggling to fall asleep lately” become “I should really see my doctor about this”?

“If it feels like a problem to you, it’s worth having a conversation about,” says Meers. Whether you’re overly tired during the daytime, feel like you can’t sleep long or well enough, or just unhappy with your sleep in one way or another, that’s reason enough to ask for help, she says.

And how do you know if you really have insomnia? Is there a line where sleep troubles become clinical?

“Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, waking up too early, or just having really poor, unrefreshing sleep. There are no guidelines on how long it takes you to fall asleep or how…
items.t: So You Think You Have Insomnia. What Now?

items.title: School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray
items.summary:
In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a new building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school. 

When my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a big deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day? 

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

What are the School Nutrition Standards? 

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by…
items.t: School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray

items.title: I Travel With A Kid Who Has Severe Allergies. Here Are The Things I Never Thought To Worry About

Anchiy/E+/Getty Images My son has severe allergies, asthma, and celiac disease, so everyday things can sometimes send us to the hospital. And traveling adds another layer of uncertainty. A hotel room that looks clean could be holding fragrances that trigger respiratory symptoms. The swimming pool down the hall could pose problemsThat gluten-free item on the menu during our family night out could be cross-contaminated. As a parent, I’ve learned that keeping my son safe means thinking beyond the obvious risks.

With the colder weather settling in and holiday travel approaching, I knew it was time to take a closer look at what families like mine should be considering before hitting the road or boarding a plane. So, I chatted with experts Dr. Sarah Beebe, a travel advisor and autism travel professional based in Lewes, Delaware, and Dr. Tracy Tyson, a pediatrician with 20 years experience in urgent care, who helped me identify the less obvious triggers families might encounter while traveling—and how to better prepare for them.

The Allergic Kid Through the colder months and when planning trips, I’d always assumed that keeping my son’s inhaler on hand was enough. I researched all of the common triggers, such as dust, pet dander, pollen, smoke and weather changes. After chatting with Dr. Tyson and Dr. Beebe, I learned of the lesser-known hazards that can lurk in the places we stay and the ways we travel.

Regarding Polly Hudson’s article (At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now, 15 November), I met and lived with a 35-year-old man when I was 17. It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference.

items.title: “Financially, I Regret Having My Third Child” & 61 Other Anonymous Mom Confessions
items.summary:
Natalia Lebedinskaia/Getty Images As we barrel towards December, money is top of mind for a lot of moms. And, really, that makes sense any year: the holidays are expensive . As moms, we’re always doing the math in our heads: how much we can afford, how much we need to cut, how much is going out vs. how much is coming in. And this year, a lot of moms are finding that the math just ain’t mathing . That theme kept surfacing in this week’s roundup of anonymous confessions. 

One mom wants a divorce but says that, in this economy, it isn’t possible. Another admits that, financially, she regrets having her third child. One mom got laid off and one mom is tired of working her ass off yet always feeling broke, and one mom, in her own words, just wants to be left alone with a lot of money. 

The cost of everything is dictating a lot right now, and moms are really feeling that. 

Then there are the other confessions that showed up this week, the kind that bubble up every week. Worries about being a good parent. Health concerns. Perimenopause ( always perimenopause !). Little wins that moms need to share with someone. 

So, here are this week’s confessions, shared anonymously by moms yelling into the void about everything from money to marriage. 

Scary Mommy Confessions are a tried-and-true part of what makes our site so fun. If you want to anonymously confess, look for our weekly callouts on Instagram . And to browse past Confessions, take a look here .

items.title: Holidays In The '90s Vs. Holidays Today: One Thing We Wish We Could Bring Back
items.summary:
Remember when the biggest holiday flex wasn't a new gaming console, but having your very own phone? Bonus points if it came with a ridiculously long cord stretching from the kitchen to your bedroom, where you'd whisper about your crush while your mom yelled at you to get off the line.

Ah, the '90s. A simpler time, when holiday wish lists were filled with digital pets, inflatable furniture, and scented stickers. We'd spend winter break watching holiday movies on cable, making plans with friends, and calling Grandma to recount everything Santa brought us. And somehow, without smartphones, we stayed pretty connected.

Fast-forward to today, and while some things have changed for the better (goodbye, dial-up internet), there's one tradition that deserves a comeback: the good old-fashioned phone call.

Enter MyPhone by Ooma, a modern, screen-free landline for kids who want independence and parents who aren't ready to hand over a smartphone. MyPhone uses internet home phone service and is easy to activate, so families don’t need an existing traditional landline connection. With more than 20 years of experience in home phone technology, you know that Ooma’s credibility is A+. And where does that matter more than with your kids?

MyPhone costs $99.99, with service priced at $7.99/month, plus taxes and fees.

Here's why this nostalgic throwback might be just what the holidays ordered.
